title: Cocaine smuggler avoids prison sentence, as judge seeks to keep child out of foster care
summary: A man who played a pivotal role in smuggling more than three kilograms of cocaine into Newfoundland has staved off a federal prison sentence, as a judge sought to keep the man's son from going into…

image.caption: An Ontario judge has sentenced a convicted drug smuggler to house arrest to avoid his son going into foster care. (Shutterstock)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

A man who played a pivotal role in smuggling more than three kilograms of cocaine into Newfoundland has staved off a federal prison sentence, as a judge sought to keep the man's son from going into foster care.
Justice Louis Strezos hopes sentence can help avoid intergenerational cycle
Steven Armstrong will spend two years less a day on house arrest, to be followed by three years of probation, in what Justice Louis Strezos admitted was an "extraordinary result."

Armstrong has become a single father in the years since his arrest for drug trafficking in 2020. The court heard his son has exceptional needs, and Armstrong is the only person capable of caring for him.
"This is a difficult sentencing decision," reads the first line of the judge's ruling.

The Crown had initially been seeking a sentence of up to seven years in prison, arguing Armstrong was not eligible for house arrest due to the nature of the offence and a lengthy criminal record for drug-related offences.
Prosecutor Christopher Kalantzis lowered his recommendation to four-to-five years after Armstrong's two co-accused were sentenced in Newfoundland and Labrador.

blocks.text: Dion Wilson Lee Rodgers was given a 39-month penitentiary term, while Edmond Dorman Pickett received 34 months.
Strezos agreed with Kalantzis that on the surface of the case, Armstrong should not be eligible for a conditional sentence order — more commonly referred to as house arrest.
"Ordinarily, he would be correct," the judge wrote.
Caring for boy is rehabilitative, judge says

However, Strezos accepted arguments from Armstrong's lawyer, Adam Boni, about how a prison sentence would be destructive to Armstrong's son, and put him in the same child welfare system that played a significant role in his father's criminality.

Steven Armstrong grew up without a father. His mother died by suicide when he was young. He was raised in group homes, where he became addicted to drugs. His criminal record started as a youth and continued up to 2011, when he was given a three-year prison sentence for drug trafficking.

items: Cocaine smuggler could avoid prison as judge fears incarceration would orphan man's son

blocks.text: Strezos also accepted Boni's argument that caring for his son has had a significant impact on Armstrong's life, kickstarting the process of rehabilitation long before a sentence was imposed.

"[The boy] has contributed to ending the cycle of the offender's criminality. Mr. Armstrong has been and will continue to be rehabilitated by caring for [him] — the 'twist of fate' aptly described by Mr. Boni," Strezos wrote.
The judge also considered letters of support, including ones from Armstrong's aunt and the boy's doctor.

"If Steven were to go to jail, it would be very detrimental to [his son] in my opinion," wrote Joan Armstrong. "Steven and [his son] are joined at the hip. I worry that the emotional toll on [him] would cause him serious harm, and cause him to regress."

"I would strongly support the possibility of house arrest rather than Steven being away from parenting time with [his son] over these important years of [his] development," the unnamed pediatrician wrote.
RCMP takedown a year in the making
Police had been watching Armstrong for more than a year before his arrest in September of 2020.

Court records show the investigation began as a probe into a central Newfoundland man and his criminal associates in 2019. During the investigation, police noticed Armstrong had made multiple short trips to the island.

Armstrong was stopped during one of those visits in 2019, but police failed to find any drugs in his vehicle. Investigators continued tracking Armstrong into 2020, when they learned he planned to transport a pickup truck to Newfoundland. The province went into lockdown in March due to the COVID-19 pandemic, leaving Armstrong unable to gain entry.

In September 2020, police followed Armstrong as he left Ontario in a 2006 Honda Ridgeline. He left the truck in a Canadian Tire parking lot in North Sydney, N.S., where Rodgers and his stepfather picked it up and drove it back to Newfoundland.
Police found 3.4 kilograms of cocaine hidden inside the truck's passenger side airbag compartment.
Judge gives warning to Armstrong
Strezos concluded a total of five years supervision — two on house arrest and three on probation — is proportionate given the "unique circumstances of this case."
The sentence will include GPS monitoring, close geographic confinement when Armstrong is not at home, some tailored exceptions and reporting to Strezos every six months.
Armstrong must also submit a DNA sample and is prohibited from owning weapons for the rest of his life.
The judge's ruling ended with a warning.
"Mr. Armstrong, I assure you that if you breach any term of this sentence, you will go to prison."
